Historical means "of, relating to, or connected with history or the past."

When you call something "historical," you are saying it has some link to real past events, real past people, real past times, or to the study of those things. The word signals that something belongs to — or is connected to — the world of the past as it actually happened.

1. Something that existed in or belongs to the past

When you say something is "historical," you often simply mean it is from a past time — it is real and it has a place in history.

"Abraham Lincoln is a historical figure."
"The French Revolution is a historical event."

Here, "historical" just means the person or event was real and belongs to history. It is not imaginary. It is not legend. It actually happened or actually existed.

2. Connected to the study or subject of history

"Historical" can describe anything that relates to history as a field of knowledge — research, methods, records, documents, analysis.

"The researcher used historical evidence to support her argument."
"He spent years doing historical research in old archives."
"The professor offered a historical perspective on modern politics."

In these cases, you are describing something as belonging to the domain of studying or examining the past.

3. Based on real past events (especially in literature and art)

A very common use is to describe creative works — novels, films, dramas — that are set in a real historical period and attempt to recreate that time.

"I love reading historical fiction."
"They made a historical drama about the Mughal Empire."
"The film was praised for its historical accuracy."

A "historical novel" is one that takes place in a real era from the past and tries to reflect the events, customs, and atmosphere of that time. The word tells you the work is rooted in history, even if some details are imagined.

4. Recorded in history; verified and real (as opposed to mythological or fictional)

"Historical" is also used to contrast something real from something imaginary or legendary.

"Was King Arthur a historical person or a myth?"
"There is no historical evidence that this event ever took place."
"The historical record shows that the city was destroyed in 410 CE."

When someone says a person is "historical," they mean that person genuinely existed — confirmed by records, artifacts, or evidence — rather than being invented in a story or legend.

5. Data or information from the past

In practical, everyday, and professional language, "historical" is used to describe information or data that was collected or relevant in a past period, as opposed to current information.

"The bank reviewed its historical data to identify trends."
"Compare the historical prices of this product with today's prices."
"Looking at historical patterns can help us predict future behavior."

This is simply a way of saying the data is from the past, not from the present.

This is one of the most important things to understand, and many people confuse these two words. They look almost the same, but they mean different things.

"Historical" simply means connected to history or the past. It is a neutral, descriptive word. It does not say anything about importance or fame.

"a historical document" → a document from or about the past

"Historic" means famous, significant, or important in history — or likely to be remembered in the future.

"a historic document" → a document that is so important it made history

More examples to make this clear:

  • "a historical building" → a building from the past, connected to history
  • "a historic building" → a famous or landmark building, celebrated for its importance
  • "a historical moment" → a moment that occurred in the past
  • "a historic moment" → a moment that was so significant, it will be remembered in history
  • "a historical figure" → a person who lived in the past
  • "a historic figure" → a person who was tremendously important in history

Think of it this way: historical is about connection to the past, while historic is about importance or fame. Everything historic is also historical, but not everything historical is historic. An ordinary blacksmith who lived in medieval England is a historical figure, but not a historic one.

Here are common combinations with "historical" and what they mean:

  • Historical context — the background circumstances of a past time that help explain why something happened.
  • Historical record — the body of documents, artifacts, and accounts that preserves knowledge of the past.
  • Historical accuracy — how faithfully something (a film, a book, a claim) reflects what actually happened.
  • Historical significance — the importance of something in the story of history.
  • Historical evidence — proof or information drawn from the past to support a claim.
  • Historical perspective — a way of understanding something by looking at how it developed over time.
  • Historical fiction — stories set in a real past period, blending real history with invented characters or events.
  • Historical analysis — the careful examination of past events, often to understand causes, effects, and meaning.

"Historical" does not mean "old."
The word is about connection to history, not about age alone. A book written yesterday about ancient Rome is a book on historical events. A very old grocery list found in someone's attic is old, but it might not be considered "historical" in any meaningful sense unless it connects to something worth studying in the past.

"Historical" is a neutral word.
It carries no judgment about whether something was good or bad, important or unimportant. It simply says: this belongs to or relates to the past.

"Historical" implies reality.
When something is described as "historical," there is usually an implication that it was real — it actually happened or existed. This is why historians debate whether figures like Homer (the Greek poet) were truly "historical persons" or largely mythological.

Historical as an adjective means: of, relating to, or based on real past events, real past people, or the study of the past. It connects something to history — either because it belongs to a past time, because it is based on real past events, because it is drawn from the study of the past, or because it is confirmed by historical record as actually having existed or occurred.

The one distinction to always keep sharp: historical = connected to the past; historic = important or famous in history.
